Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette: Two years ago, Dina was contracted to deep-clean a vacant luxury penthouse after hours. When a squatter breached the service entrance, the confrontation escalated quickly. He grabbed her wrists, pinned her against the marble counter, and screamed that she would leave or he would call the authorities on her. Every movement was dictated by his commands. She was forced to drop her cleaning caddy, forced to back toward the window, forced to remain silent while he rifled through drawers. The assault was brief, but the suffocating compliance left a visceral imprint that would later dictate how she navigated the world. In the weeks that followed, Dina’s recall of that night refused to settle into a coherent whole. Certain fragments burned with terrifying precision—the exact chime of the deadbolt, the smell of damp wool on his jacket—while the rest of the evening remained a hollowed-out void. She often caught herself tracing the dull, throbbing ache across her forearms whenever the images surfaced, the phantom pain flaring exactly where his grip had bruised her. This fractured recall made the past feel unresolved and dangerously near. When the incomplete picture of the event resurfaced during quiet moments, it acted like a key, unlocking a sudden, visceral spike of alarm whenever she encountered anything remotely similar. The fragmented memories themselves became catalysts, pulling her attention sharply toward environmental cues she had once ignored. Her work as a housekeeper, once a steady rhythm of familiar routines, quickly became a minefield. One Tuesday, a client’s husband stormed into the living room, his voice rising in a sharp shout over a misplaced invoice. Dina flinched so hard her spray bottle clattered to the floor. The shouted volume bypassed her reasoning and tapped directly into her nervous system, flooding her with an immediate, body-deep alert. The sound of raised voices now acted as a direct ignition switch for her threat state, bypassing any sense of safety. Similarly, being asked to rearrange her cleaning cart or follow sudden, abrupt instructions from property managers triggered a cold tightness in her chest, as if she were back under someone else’s command. Even seeing news reports about residential break-ins or hearing other clients talk about past burglaries would suddenly tighten her shoulders, as if the memories of other victims were being pulled into her immediate periphery. That constant trigger-response loop kept her in a permanent state of high alert. Dina stopped entering rooms without first sweeping her eyes across every corner and window, her gaze constantly scanning for hidden figures or unusual shadows. At night, the silence of her own bedroom became unbearable; she would lie still, straining her ears to catch the faintest creak of the floorboards or the scratch of a key in the front lock, convinced that safety was only as fragile as her next breath. This relentless vigilance fractured her focus during work hours. She found herself dropping sponges mid-wipe or forgetting entire steps of her checklist, not from carelessness but from the sheer cognitive load of trying to filter out every potential threat. The more she scanned and monitored her environment, the more the world felt populated with hidden dangers, which in turn made her hypersensitive to any sudden shout or abrupt demand, ensuring the alarm never fully quieted. The cumulative toll became impossible to ignore. Her husband, Amir, noticed how she slept with the porch light on and how she jumped at the delivery bell, but his reassurances only seemed to widen the gap between them. She was no longer able to relax during their evening meals, her mind constantly dissecting the sounds of their street for anything that might precede an intrusion. The professional consequences followed swiftly; a property manager finally noted her recent errors in attendance and concentration, placing her on a formal warning. It was the combination of that warning and a panic attack in a grocery store aisle—triggered by a stock clerk’s raised voice—that finally pushed Dina to sit across from a clinician. She did not want the constant scanning or the phantom pains, but what frightened her most was losing the very coping structures she had built, even though they were slowly isolating her from the life she loved.
